The government has missed a golden opportunity with Bill C-48 to provide a clear signal to the small businessmen of Canada that it recognizes their role, that it wants to encourage them, to support their efforts by building in to the program a
Canada Oil and Gas Act
very sophisticated, sound and strong "buy Canada" procurement policy. Why not "buy Canada" when it comes to the megaprojects planned for our country? Why not buy goods and services from Canadians rather than foreigners wherever possible?
I do not want to suggest for a moment that the purchasing agents of multinational oil companies are ogres or are insensitive. After all, these are usually people from Dallas and Houston who have come up to Calgary and Edmonton and farther north to lnuvik, Aklavik, and Tuktoyaktuk to do business. They need equipment, and their natural inclination is to contact their friends and colleagues in Houston and Chicago when they want to buy. It is the old boy system where you help out your friends.
When foreigners are making the decisions about procurement in Canada, it is not surprising that they look to their friends in the United States and to Germany and to Japan. We in the NDP ask why that should not be changed and a "buy Canada" policy made part of Bill C-48 to require that, whenever possible, goods and services be purchased from Canadian suppliers.
Incredible sums of money will be involved in servicing equipment in the north. In the next decade $210 billion will be spent on developing northern Canada.
Most of it outside the country.

Most of it outside the country, as my colleague says. The Royal Bank of Canada estimates that in the next 20 years in excess of $1 trillion will be spent developing megaprojects and exploring Canada lands. The unfortunate thing is that most of that $1 trillion will go to foreign suppliers. But that need not be the case, Mr. Speaker. We know that 85 per cent of the cost of exploration could come from Canadian sources. We also know that 90 per cent of all equipment for refineries could come from Canadian manufacturers, although at the moment only 30 per cent comes from Canadian manufacturers.
Canada is recognized as being quite sophisticated in the areas of training and education. We probably have one of the best educated populations in the world, yet most of the people in the engineering consortiums responsible for the engineering on the megaprojects come from San Francisco, Los Angeles, Detroit or Chicago. Surely the government has an obligation to provide the leadership necessary to pull together our own engineering expertise in order to develop our own resources?
Most of the labour used on our pipeline construction comes from Canada, but most of the equipment does not. About 60 per cent of the equipment used on Canadian pipelines is imported from the United States and other countries. Virtually all of this equipment could be manufactured and supplied in Canada, Mr. Speaker. Much of the skilled labour that will be required to develop Canada lands will have to be imported because the Liberal government did not plan to develop the expertise required for these projects.

November 9, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
The opposition parties put a lot of work into amendments to Bill C-48, Mr. Speaker. Of course, the government did accept eight changes. It changed the bill in eight ways, but then we must ask who benefited from those changes. You can bet it was not the native people of northern Canada, it was not the governments of northern Canada it was not the northern environment and it was not the small businesses in northern or southern Canada; predictably, the large corporations benefited. Changes were made for their back-in clauses, royalties were reduced and tax-escape clauses were introduced. All the changes were to help the large corporations, mainly foreign corporations operating in Canada's north. Of course, when one thinks about it, what could one expect from a government that refused even to go into the north and talk to those people who were to be directly affected by this legislation?
One of the myths which is perpetuated in this House almost every time someone from the Tory party stands up to speak is the extent to which we need this foreign investment, that it is absolutely mandatory for foreign companies to become involved in our oil industry. The surprising thing is that Canada is unique in the world. Canada is one of the only oil producing countries in the world that has not taken bold steps to control and own its petroleum industry. We are unique. We are a world leader. We have sold out more than any other country in the world. One can take a look around. Great Britain has taken a major step with its British National Oil Corporation. This corporation has first claim on 51 per cent of the share of the oil production off Great Britain's coast. Its purchase is negotiated at market prices. The BNOC may offer participation to joint venture partners, including foreign-owned firms, but it retains control of all projects. I think it is important, as my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, indicated, that it may change control, not only ownership, but certainly control must be the important thing.
Sell it all.

Norway now has new gas finds off its north coast and substantial deposits off its western and southern coasts. In Norway, Statoil, the government oil company, can take up to a 70 per cent interest in any block of land that it does not already hold. Statoil takes this interest after a find but before development, and makes no payment at all for past exploration expenditures. Yet we hear a howling and a yowling from the Tories, particularly, saying that this particular Bill C-48 is an expropriation bill. It takes from the oil companies. Takes what from the oil companies? Does it take the natural gas and oil from the oil companies? I think it begs the question: who is it that owns that oil and gas now? Of course it is the people of Canada who own that oil and gas. We are simply saying that it is time that we developed these resources ourselves and that the benefits stayed in this country.
What about Australia? Certainly Australia is recognized as being one of the free enterprise countries of the world, but foreign companies are allowed to explore there. However, only Australian and naturalized foreign investors are allowed to
produce energy from the resources, even in Australia. What about Mexico? We import oil from Mexico. Mexico took care of its situation there many, many years ago, back in 1939, and has nationalized its oil company.
Yes, we are a leader. We have sold out this strategic resource more than any other producing country in the world. We in the New Democratic Party are not very pleased at that prospect, and we feel it is time that major steps were taken to obtain control once again over that particular resource.
Let us go back to the myth that foreign oil companies are required to bring capital into this country. I think that we cannot overstate it. My colleague, the hon. member for Van-couver-Kingsway, has mentioned many, many times that the oil industry policy in Canada results in a net export of capital out of Canada. Our oil industries are net capital exporters. They do not bring money into the country, in spite of all the glossy ads that we see taken out in our national newspapers, again to justify what no other country producing oil and natural gas has accepted. Net capital outflows between 1975 and 1979, the last years for which we have statistics, amounted to $2.1 billion. If one were to add the dividends and interest payments that also left the country during that same four-year period, we would find that a total of $3.7 billion flowed out of Canada, a net export of capital of $3.7 billion.
Surely that should put to rest some of the arguments that we cannot do it ourselves and that we depend upon foreign investor in this particular sector. I will be the first one to say that we ought to welcome foreign investors and expertise of any kind. But surely it is time that Canada took major steps to ensure that this strategic resource is understood and controlled by Canada.
It is a sad day when people ask us, "How much natural gas do we really have left? How much oil do we really have?" It is sad when we have to respond that we do not know because we do not control it. The oil companies know how much natural gas and oil they have under their leases, and they are not telling each other. They are certainly not telling the rest of Canada. I think it is a sad day when such a strategic resource is controlled in a fragmented way by foreign capital.
Another myth, of course, is that the national energy policy is resulting in a major Canadianization of our industry, a major step toward Canadianization. I think it is important that we continue to emphasize that 65 per cent of our industry remains foreign controlled. It is something that, again, we in this party simply will not accept, and we will keep fighting until that percentage point is considerably reduced.
Another myth we keep hearing about is that the PetroCan Company of Canada is becoming too powerful. Even with Petrofina acquisitions, PetroCan ranks as Canada's eighth largest oil producer and Canada's third largest natural gas producer. Up to this point, we were quite proud of that. Unlike our Tory friends, we feel proud, for example, when we drive into our PetroCan stations.
I must say that when I go into the various stations around my riding and ask the operators how they are doing, they are
November 9, 1981

very pleased. Their business is up and growing. When one goes into a PetroCan station, one is investing in one's own company. It is not a foreign oil company that one is serving. It seems to me that this will be a challenge for Petro-Canada in the future. We must be different from the others. Petro-Canada must be accountable to the people of Canada. Petro-Canada must operate in a very businesslike manner. We must be very careful, as my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, has indicated, that it is not run by Liberal hacks, as we see all too often when it comes to Crown corporations, and that it does not start the corporate jetsetting about the country typical of so many of the private oil companies.
Here is an opportunity for Canada, endorsed by the people of Canada, to develop new techniques and new energy fields, to use Petro-Canada as an opportunity to move into the use of methane gas and hydrogen, and geothermal energy. It should be more than simply an oil and gas company, because I do not think there is anyone in this chamber who would say that oil and gas as a critical, strategic resource will be around much longer. The price will simply not be there. We have to move into other areas. We have to be innovative and take some real initiative to move into the development of new energy technologies. Surely, Petro-Canada provides us with that ready vehicle to move into wind energy, methane gas, hydrogen, geothermal energy, and on and on, and to take that initiative. We should see it as an energy company, not simply as an oil and gas company.
In closing, I would like to say that we in the New Democratic Party are disappointed that the progressive amendments which we put forward were not considered and given a fair hearing. We will continue to struggle to ensure that the next time a bill like Bill C-48 comes before us, it will mean something, and it will take into consideration the sensitivity of the northern and other environments, and that it will be sensitive to the people who will be directly influenced by the bill, such as the Inuit, Indians, Metis, and governments of northern Canada. It is time that the government became more sensitive along all these lines, but the fact that it is not is not surprising. Why should it become sensitive now? This government has shown an incredible insensitivity to westerners. Look at the recent decisions on VIA Rail. One could say it has an insensitivity to easterners, as well. It has an insensitivity when it comes to supporting economic infrastructure in western Canada. It is not surprising that once again through Bill C-48 the Liberal government has shown an insensitivity to the people and to the environment of northern Canada.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: What about provincial status?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak on third reading of Bill C-48. Some months ago we had second reading. As members of the opposition, we raised quite a number of points upon which we were opposed in principle. We identified these issues, such as the confiscation provisions, the ministerial discretion provisions and those types of provisions enabling a minister and a bureaucracy in Ottawa to direct where a well is to be drilled. They might be good people, but may not have the technical skills or the expertise and, because of some political consideration, may direct a company to drill in spot A rather than in spot B, whereas the well should be drilled based on seismic evidence.
We pointed out that the amount of land given to Petro-Canada under the principle of the bill would be grossly
excessive, it being 135 million acres. We raised the issue of the treatment of the Yukoners as a people and the people in the Northwest Territories and their aspirations toward provincial status.
Those of us who live in the west, and particularly those of us who come from Alberta, know of the incredible battles that had to be fought before we achieved ownership of our resources. Indeed, it took us 25 years to achieve that end. Do hon. members opposite realize that it was 1930 when we finally achieved ownership? A Liberal provincial government fought from 1905 to 1921 for this right, but it was unsuccessful and it was turfed out of office by the people. The UFA party in 1924 actually debated a resolution to separate from Canada. That is how deeply westerners felt about the issue. The resolution was defeated, but Alberta was successful within six years after that and achieved ownership of resources. I believe that is why we in this party have a greater sensitivity toward the aspirations of the people in the Yukon and in the Northwest Territories. That matter was raised at second reading as being one we should want to follow up at committee stage, at report stage and at third reading.
Our party has raised the question of self-sufficiency in oil. We dealt with that. As hon. members know, the bill went to committee as is the practice after second reading. I believe some 35 witnesses appeared before the committee. Many changes were proposed by expert witnesses, interested parties and the environmentalists who appeared before the committee. As a result, the government itself proposed over 100 amendments to the bill. That has to tell you something about the initial drafting of the bill, Mr. Speaker. It is somewhat like the constitutional resolution which one would have expected to have been well thought out and drafted. Instead, it required dozens and dozens of amendments by the government side to correct poor draftmanship, poorly thought out ideas and concepts. The same thing occurred with Bill C-48. I believe the government itself made over 100 changes. Our party, the official opposition and the New Democratic Party proposed many changes as well, the vast majority of which were not accepted by the government. We moved on to the report stage which we dealt with recently. We had 57 motions which were dealt with in over 30 votes. Those amendments were not amendments that were put forth for narrow partisan reasons. Many of the amendments were justifiable as a matter of logic and concern, whether it be for the sake of the environment or the definition of a spill or the type of notice we give to the native peoples of the north.
I am really disappointed that the government would not have some mechanism whereby those amendments could be genuinely considered and some of them accepted. The report stage is the time when ordinary Members of Parliament become involved with members on the government side in a process, whether it be in a special caucus on the government side or in full caucus, whereby amendments are genuinely considered by the ordinary members. What happens is that the minister and his bureaucracy become so committed to the bill
November 9, 1981

they really lose their sense of judgment, of being able to recognize what is reasonable. I think ordinary backbenchers, if they have genuinely studied this issue and are informed, would then say: That is a reasonable amendment, why not accept it? If that were so, it would make the whole process of government at the federal level much more responsive to the genuine needs of this whole large country. I am sure we would all agree that no one person or bureaucracy can get a real grasp of this country and the intricate needs of small regions. I am disappointed the government has not done that, but I hope it will at some point in the future.
Why did the government reject these opposition amendments? Why was there no movement on confiscation, on ministerial discretion, on the amount of land that is covered and on the treatment of Yukoners? I do not know the answer. I believe the government members who come to the House should take more time and give genuine thought to the legislation the cabinet and the bureaucracy put forth. If that does not occur, then this House and our government, with a cabinet and a bureaucracy which are supposed to be responsible to the whole House and its members, are not fulfilling their function, and party loyalty is far too great a concern on the part of members.
Perhaps we should change our rules so that if a government is defeated on a motion to amend a bill, it will not reflect on the question of whether the government has to resign. This should clearly be a free vote and the government should be able to say, "Okay, members, you are not happy with that. We will take it back, work on it again, change it and carry on." It would then be only on major bills, the budget, the throne speech and some major pieces of legislation that a government would have to fall. On these ordinary bills that would not be the case. Hon. members who come from the Arctic and the Yukon really know what will work in the north, so their opinion should clearly be worth more and should be listened to.
We are now at third reading stage, and I want to make it clear that I certainly disagree with the bill and will have no hesitation at all in voting against it. I want to set forth once again the major reasons I am opposed to the Canada oil and gas act, Bill C-48.
First of all, we know the area of land we are dealing with is that vast territory off the west coast of B.C., all the northern territories and the area off the east coast to the extent the federal government has jurisdiction. It encompasses 135 million acres. That amount of land is greater than all the land in the world that Exxon is involved with.
It is half of Canada.

Is that not amazing? As the hon. member points out, it is half of Canada. That is more land than Exxon is involved with in the entire world. As the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) points out, if Petro-Canada were to bring on sufficient staff, geologists, engineers and physicists, in the same proportion as Exxon has done, in order to deal with that amount of land it would have to have a building in Calgary one square block and 854 storeys high.
Canada Oil and Gas Act
Don't tell them that, they will build it.
Oh, oh!
And they will populate it, too.
Oh, oh!
And the taxpayer will pay for it.

That shows how patently impossible this is. Therefore, we have to ask how they are going to develop that land. I suppose the answer is that the government is either going to buy out other multinational corporations, about which I will have a few words to say, or it will develop more Crown corporations from scratch to go in and develop that land. This is a great potential for Canadian companies but, unfortunately, as a result of the National Energy Program, the government has virtually forced many of the active and creative Canadian companies out of the country because there is a better deal for them elsewhere.
My second reason is the 25 per cent confiscation provision. That rule applies not only to non-Canadians but to Canadians as well. I suppose if it applied only to non-Canadians, we might say we should try it once and if we get away with it, that is fine. Very likely we would get away with it because the government has systematically built a case against the multinational oil companies, making them appear evil in the minds of the ordinary Canadian citizens. That is a misconception because multinational corporations are as much a part of this world and will be as we are ourselves. We have an incredible number of multinational corporations, including Petro-Canada.
The minister of energy wants Petro-Canada to be all over the world. It is involved in the Norwegian Sea, in the Far East and off Mexico. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) wants it to be able to go to Tanzania, as he did, so he can say, "We will have our state oil company come in with $250 million." So PetroCan is a multinational corporation.
If we expect to expropriate or confiscate 25 per cent of non-Canadian companies, we should surely expect that same type of conduct to occur in other countries. What kind of example is that for the Canadian government to set for the rest of the world? When they start taking 25 per cent of Petro-Canada's assets in Tanzania, or 25 per cent of the assets in Norway, Switzerland, or wherever they might be, we will not be very happy. There is no way around it, the 25 per cent confiscation rule is just theft, pure and simple.
The rationale used is that the government gave tax deductions, super-depletion and, therefore, that it is justifiable. If that is so, then surely the government could take over all farms because they are very important and farmers have had tax deductions. All of us must surely be slaves because we have personal exemptions, marital exemptions and child exemptions. The rationale is wrong as a matter of principle. Surely we would want to take over children, because they are very important.

November 9, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
The hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) seemed to indicate that because oil was so strategic, the government had to have state control of it. I suppose nothing is more important than farms, so we better take them over. We cannot entrust children to their ordinary mortal parents, so the NDP would surely want the government to take them over. What about clothing? We could never leave the manufacturing of clothing to ordinary Canadian companies. That is just too important. Man needs to have homes, clothing and food. We would then take over the food. We would have to take over clothing, and then, by God, we would be in dress uniforms, as they are in some countries, because the bureaucracy would find that a common uniform would tend to make us more unified. Then I could not come swinging in from the west in my western suit because that would be embarrassing for some chap here. We would all wear a common red outfit, I presume.
This confiscation is not the Canadian way. It is not something we want to start. It is not something with which we want to inculcate in our children, the idea that the government can take advantage of creative people coming in and investing their money by taking it away from them. It is not a concept we want to promote.
I will now turn to the third major reason why I am opposed to this bill. That reason is simply the incapacity of Crown corporations, such as Petro-Canada, to act as a creative, searching force in the oil and gas industry. The oil and gas industry is far too technical and complicated for a Crown corporation to be involved in. It is not a utility, such as a dam on a river from which you obtain hydro power. That is there all the time. The oil and gas industry needs enthusiastic searchers who have to do complicated exploration and seismic work. It needs specially skilled people to take part in the production of wells and to develop them. Oil is not just sitting there in a pool under the ground; it is locked into the sand and shale. We need people with incredible skills to lift it to the surface and maintain it so the wells are not watering out; people who can get a 60 per cent or 70 per cent return from a pool of oil rather than just 30 per cent.
1 am thoroughly convinced that it is impossible for a Crown corporation to achieve that. I am not saying that the people within the Crown corporation are incompetent, but because of our democratic system of government, that system will grind them down. An example of that is the Post Office. There is nothing wrong with the individuals who work there but because of the system of responding to politics, they are incapable of performing their function. Recently we wrote off $800 million to the CNR, and this has occurred every few years in the past. The Atomic Energy of Canada corporation is another Crown corporation for which we just wrote off $600 million to make its books balance so it could be in the black. We wrote off $196 million for the CBC last year. The reason is that a Crown corporation cannot function in particular in the oil and gas industry. People like Masters and Grey who have a concept and an idea, are the real searchers. They would be stifled by the accounting process and responsibility which
they would run into in a Crown corporation and they would not last long.
What would happen once a Crown corporation was unionized as this one will be? What would happen if we had a strike and an oil well were shut down? The shut down of an oil well could interfere with the pressures of oil flow versus water, gas or steam, and the well would simply be lost. It could be a total loss and that is exactly what would happen if there were a strike. I have seen it happen in my house where the electricity, which was controlled by a provincial Crown corporation, was shut off because of a strike. The pipes in my house froze, as well as in other people's houses, and when they thawed, they blew up. Apartments had to be vacated. That is what happens when a Crown corporation has too much power. The unionized employees in Petro-Canada stations across the country will have the right under law to go on strike, and they will.
Under our system today where different companies are in competition with each other, they can be played one against the other thus making them unable to force their will on the industry to fulfil its needs.
A classic example of a Crown corporation being unable to respond to the needs in the country was the recent change that took place in the service station industry. We have gone from full service stations to self-serve. That change caused enormous difficulties for individual operators who invested their money, found it uneconomic and then went bankrupt. If those stations were owned by a Crown corporation which reports back to a minister, it would be impossible to make that change in the industry, even though it was an absolutely essential change, because its employees would all be voters who lobby through a minister and the government's reputation would be on the line. We would have to spend millions of dollars to keep those stations operating even though they were uneconomic.
Like Mirabel.
I suppose Mirabel is the classic example where something like $20,000 a day-
A million dollars a day.
A member tells me a million dollars flows into Mirabel.
Close the airports and privatize them too.

Maybe it is a good idea.
The fourth reason, carrying on this debate-
Privatize the highways while you are at it.

The hon. member is starting to work in the right way. It shows that perhaps wisdom can be achieved with advancing years.
Another reason why the government should not be involved
is that it is virtually impossible for a government to be both a
participant in an industry and a regulator. It is impossible
November 9, 1981

because it leads to a conflict of interest. As an example, when Petro-Canada bought Pacific Petroleum, it cost $1.5 billion. It did not have the money, so it went to a consortium of Canadian and U.S. banks and borrowed the $1.5 billion. They were able to give a special preference share because of the tax loophole. The deal went through on November 10. They took advantage of this tax share where the banks do not pay any tax on the interest they earned, and on November 17, seven days later, the government closed that loophole for any other Canadian company which might have wanted to take advantage of it.
When we examine that deal we find that a senior deputy minister is on the board of directors of the corporation. That is an automatic conflict of interest, and the Crown corporation took advantage of something which the other corporations could not do. Later we found that a vice president of Petro-Canada wrote the budget which gave Petro-Canada those incredible advantages over those other companies which were operating honestly and decently in the industry.
The final flowering of the practice, Mr. Speaker, has become evident recently when it was found that a minister's assistant is in the active employ of Petro-Canada even though he has never worked for the corporation, and that he is receiving mortgage benefits. It is clear that the conflict of interest becomes almost unbelievable.
I would rather see the government sit back and be the regulator. I do not care how stiff the rules are so long as they are fair for everyone. I have another example for the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Masters). The example is that of Pemex in Mexico, their national oil company. It does not have the facilities or skill to put out an oil fire. It always has to call in the multinationals because they have the skills and creativity. Red Adair goes all over the world to put out oil well fires. The national oil company of Mexico drills a well, it blows out and we have almost the entire Gulf of Mexico destroyed because of that blowout. It did not have the capacity to figure out how to stop the blowout. It did not have any regulations for it. Why would they have regulations in Mexico? The state oil company is carrying out the operation. The state oil company would not do anything against its national interest. Therefore, Mexico does not have regulations.
We find the same situation in Canada. The regulations which should operate in the industry should be strict and are strict for everyone except Petro-Canada. Petro-Canada receives preference in the the oil leases and, if that does not work, it receives a 25 per cent back-in. That does not work, so we now have the flowering of the policy which is an absolute 25 per cent confiscation. The government is going to make the company work even if it has to take every cent from every Canadian because the government's reputation is on the line. That is what happens when a Crown corporation is in an industry in which it should not be.
I will turn now to the National Energy Program because the Canada oil and gas act is really the flowering of that policy. It is a story that perhaps most members do not understand. It starts back in the 1930s and goes into the early 1970s. There
Canada Oil and Gas Act
was a conspiracy in the oil industry, and it was a conspiracy not to dupe Canadians or North Americans or Europeans; it was a conspiracy between our governments, the seven international oil sisters, against all of the producers, whether they were in Nigeria or Saudi Arabia. For 50 years we held them down so that oil came into Montreal at $2.35 a barrel. When the father of the Shah of Iran said, "That is not enough, pay us more," we cut him off at the knees. Our governments knew that and participated in it. That was wrong. We treated those people badly, and we are now going to pay for it because when they obtained economic power, they raised the price. But what had happened in the meantime was that we had designed all our infrastructure, whether it had to do with manufacturing or farming, for artificially cheap oil and petroleum. The adjustment becomes very difficult.
But did we face the adjustment? No. In 1973 and 1974 our great Liberal government said, "We are going to protect our Canadian citizens." Hon. members might say that is a good policy, but that sends a signal, and it is now spelling the doom of the automotive industry in North America. Those Canadian men and women who are out of work in Windsor and all along that corridor can relate their unemployment directly to the decision of the Liberal government in 1973 to hold down the price of oil.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext: Come on.

The hon. member should just listen because that decision sent a signal to us as Canadian citizens that we could continue to buy big cars. It sent a signal to the car manufacturers that they could continue to produce big cars. Meanwhile, in Japan and Germany where they had to go to world prices because they had no oil, they turned their skilled people, their engineers, designers and architects, to the task of energy conservation in cars and buildings. As a result, eight years later they are cleaning our clocks in the automotive industry, and it is directly the result of that Liberal policy to keep down the price of oil.
Government can hurt us; there is no doubt about it. The Liberals are masters at promising one thing and doing another, and they have definitely hurt ordinary Canadians. The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) claims to speak for ordinary Canadians. That was the message in his speech tonight. I think he honestly holds that view, but was he really speaking for Yukoners and the people in the Northwest Territories? I have not heard him speak in connection with this bill about their aspiration to provincehood and to control the wealth from their minerals.
That is what I said in my speech, exactly that.

1 did not hear that. I will be delighted to read the hon. member's speech, but that surely was not in it. Was he speaking for Canadians' controlling the oil industry? No, he was speaking for government control.

Are they not Canadians?

November 9, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act

The hon. member for Vancouver-Kinsgway and I have an honest disagreement. He honestly believes that a cabinet, a bureaucracy and a state oil company can make decisions in the best interests of ordinary Canadians whether they live in Tuktoyaktuk or St. John's.
While you think that the multinationals in Houston can make a better decision.

Multinational corporations can control the oil industry no more than they can fly to the moon. The provinces decide where they drill. Who decides whether land is available to an oil company? The provinces decide that. Who decides where they drill? The provinces decide. Who decides at what rate oil is produced? The provinces decide. Who decides the price? The federal government decides that. Who decides whether any oil is exported? The federal government decides that. The oil industry is the most controlled industry in the whole nation. We then have to ask under those circumstances what ownership really means.
Why, then, are they so eager to hold onto it, pray tell?

Ownership means absolutely nothing under those circumstances. They get a rate of return, and the rate of return has been such that 2 per cent to 3 per cent of the value of their assets leaves this country. That is the cost we pay for that capital. Under the NDP philosophy we would buy them out. It is true that we have spent $6.8 billion to buy an additional 3 per cent or 4 per cent of the oil industry. All that money has left the country. We have had to borrow the money, and the money is costing us 20 per cent. Instead of losing 2 per cent to 3 per cent on a dividend, we are losing 20 per cent on the debt equity. It is absolutely absurd. The hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap admitted tonight that we are buying an industry which is at the end of its rope. Why are we spending billions of dollars to buy an oil industry which by the year 2010 will be gone?
Will you support us if we take over the solar industry?

Why do we not instead take that money and put it into new wave technology? What did Atlantic Richfield do with the money? What did Pacific Petroleums do with its $1.5 billion, and what did Petrofina do with its $1.5 billion? They are putting it into the new wave, so that when we come to get hydrogen power and solar power, from where will we buy the energy units? We will buy them from the successor of Petrofina, and we will be holding the tail. This makes no sense, as a matter of principle. If we took $1.5 billion and put it into hydrogen research, we could then have Canadian companies leading the next wave of energy. Those are the points I and other hon. members have made right from the beginning of proceedings on this bill. I plead with hon. members opposite to use some common sense, to try to get to the minister and to get these decisions through because there are some good ideas in
what we on this side say, whether or not hon. members opposite like it.
I see my time is passing. I would like to say a few words about the monopoly power implicit in Bill C-48. It goes back to the discretionary power the minister has. We know how a minister is always controlled by his bureaucracy. Nobody can dispute that. We now see the government organizing an attack on multinational oil corporations and anything that is big and powerful. The government is organizing an attack on the newspaper industry. It is fascinating that the government should do that because the government itself is the largest monopoly and power in our whole society. The government spends five or six times more on advertising than the other major advertiser in Canada. I think Proctor and Gamble spends $24 million a year on advertising, and the Government of Canada spends about $125 million a year. Do we ever see the government trying to stop its own growth? If it did bring in genuine combines legislation, the government would be stopping itself. How will Petro-Canada handle 132 million acres of Canada? That would make Petro-Canada such a powerful corporation that it would be a world and law unto itself. Why does the government not look at itself and break itself down? Why does its competition law not apply to government rules as well?
This bill will have an effect on the business climate. Its 25 per cent confiscatory dimension has virtually destroyed our reputation in the international field, and there is no doubt that that has occurred and will affect us for many years. We as Canadians cannot afford that because we still have a small population of only 23 million people stretched out over the assets and resources of half a continent. In Canada there is more land per person than anywhere in the entire world. Because of our unique cultural and historic development, most of us are the decendants of immigrants. Most of our ancestors were poor and did not have capital. Canadians got into the habit of putting their money into banks. The banks then invest it by lending to corporations which did business. As a result, we do not have enough incentive or desire within ourselves to get out and take risks. The Americans have this. That is something we could be stimulating. It was occurring in the oil and gas industry until bill C-48 came along. Most of the companies taking over the gas industry, at least in Alberta, were Canadian-owned companies. They were often men and women who had worked for multinationals, saw the chance to get out, went out and incorporated their own companies, hired their own searchers and engineers and became Canadian corporations doing the drilling because again the multinationals do not-
Call it ten o'clock.

subtopic: MARINE TRANSPORT-MINISTER'S POSITION RESPECTING CAST SHIPPING GROUP. B) REQUEST FOR GENERAL INQUIRY INTO EAST COAST SHIPPING
MARINE TRANSPORT-MINISTER'S POSITION RESPECTING CAST SHIPPING GROUP. B) REQUEST FOR GENERAL INQUIRY INTO EAST COAST SHIPPING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question to which 1 want to address some remarks this evening was raised in this chamber on June 30, 1981. It involved an inquiry to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) concerning the relationship of the Canadian National Railways Company with the Cast shipping group. The relationship between CN and Cast and my concern about it goes back in time to January 1981 when I first raised the question with the Minister of Transport.
At that time I was concerned about a very substantial investment by CN in the Cast shipping group in the area of $50 million. It had come to public knowledge that these funds were being used to purchase or construct ships in foreign shipyards, particularly Korea and Yugoslavia. Other funds were being used to purchase equipment abroad. This is a major concern in relation to Canada's shipbuilding industry and Canadian manufacturing in general.
The minister indicated in January 1981 that he thought the CN investment in Cast was a very valuable one for that transportation company and for Canadians. It followed subsequently that the concern in relation to the Cast-CN arrangement became relevant to events in the port of Halifax. In particular, in February 1981 one of the major users of the Halterm container pier in the port of Halifax announced they were leaving the port to utilize the port of Montreal. That company was the Dart Container Line. Their departure from the port of Halifax became a matter of major and serious concern. Subsequently and more recently, in September 1981, another major user of the port of Halifax, Trans-Freight Line indicated it would discontinue its service to the port of Halifax. In part, the reasons for these business decisions was the declining activity in the North Atlantic container traffic. This is a fact of life faced by all international shipping companies.
Let me say at the outset that I firmly believe in the free enterprise system and I firmly believe that international shipping companies have the right in our system to make business decisions in accordance with their own best judgment. What is at stake here in moves like Dart and Trans-Freight Line is the application of government policies, in particular the government policy which permitted the Canadian National Railways Company, our national transportation company, to invest in the Cast shipping group. While it has a Canadian connection, it is basically a foreign-owned company.
Adjournment Debate
We are very much concerned about the role of the Canadian National Railways Company in this activity. We are not about to have the president of the Canadian National Railways Company, Mr. Robert Bandeen, tell us how to handle our affairs. I refer particularly to an article that appeared in the Halifax Mail-Star in which Mr. Bandeen indicated that politicians should stop crying and start selling the port. Of course, Mr. Bandeen was protecting himself. In fact, the substantial investment that the Canadian National Railways Company made in Cast is proving to be a very inappropriate investment for our national transportation company. Not only does it have ramifications in relation to other shipping lines, the indications are that the investment will not be productive.
At present the Canadian National Railways Company has a book value investment of some $60 million which will yield a return of approximately 7.5 per cent in respect of some of the funds, and a return of not much more than 12 per cent in respect of other funds. This is at a point in our financial history when government savings bonds yield 19 per cent interest annually. The investment itself is of serious concern to the Canadian taxpayer. More important, Mr. Speaker, and the point I raised in June and previously in January, is that there is need for a general investigation into north Atlantic container traffic, particularly in the light of these involvements between land transport companies like the Canadian National and ocean transport companies like Cast. The relationship that has developed between the Dart shipping group and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has also given rise to concerns that are now being considered by the Canadian Transport Commission.
The important point I should like to raise now is the fact that the water transport committee of the Canadian Transport Commission has ordered the Canadian National Railways Company to appear before it and show cause why this investment in the Cast shipping group should be allowed. What has the CN done? Has it complied with the request of the CTC? No; it has started an appeal against this decision and asked for a delay so that we will not be able to find out the ramifications of this investment and of the relationship between Cast and CN. The real danger for all Canadians and for Canadian transport is that we will develop into a very limited service between organizations like Cast and the CN, leaving no room for independent operators.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Bockstael (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):

subtopic: MARINE TRANSPORT-MINISTER'S POSITION RESPECTING CAST SHIPPING GROUP. B) REQUEST FOR GENERAL INQUIRY INTO EAST COAST SHIPPING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member's question refers to legislation before the U.S. Congress which would restrict the movement of U.S. bound and U.S. originating containers through Canadian ports.
Behind the hon. member's question, of course, is his well known concern for the prosperity of the Port of Halifax. He attributes the recent loss of the Dart shipping group to unfair competition from a rival container line known as Cast. The reason he raises the U.S. legislation is that Cast's aggressive

November 9, 1981
Adjournment Debate
marketing practices were mentioned during the Congressional hearings.
As far as the legislation itself is concerned, the hon. member knows that Canada sent a note to the U.S. in June, 1980, objecting to the extraterritorial nature of the legislation. Both the state and justice departments in the U.S. were heard before the subcommittee studying the legislation and expressed concerns. Although the legislation narrowly passed the subcommittee, there is no reason to assume that it will become law in the near future.
The hon. member's real concern is evidently the role of Cast and the fact that Canadian National holds an interest, albeit a minor one, in Cast. The hon. member will remember that the gentleman who criticized Cast's practices during the congressional hearings himself represented a U.S. east coast port. Since his port was in direct competition with Canadian ports, his testimony must be seen in the light of the interests he represented.
The hon. member will also remember from answers given in the House by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), from evidence presented during an opposition day debate last March, and from a number of "late shows," that the Government of Canada has shown itself to be committed to the Port of Halifax. Neither the departure of Dart, nor the recent rumours regarding Zim containers, which appear to be unfounded in any case, can in any way be traced to government actions that are alleged to discriminate against Halifax. There is no need for a special investigation since the matter is currently in the hands of the CTC, which is continuing its investigation.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to reiterate this commitment and share the optimism of many of the people in the Halifax port community regarding the future of their port.

subtopic: METRIC CONVERSION-SUGGESTED PENALTIES FOR FOOD STORE OWNERS
METRIC CONVERSION-SUGGESTED PENALTIES FOR FOOD STORE OWNERS
speechtext:
On Wednesday, November 4, I rose in the House and asked the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) if he would withdraw the order in council which specifically states that as of certain dates in 1982 it is the intention of the Consumer and Corporate Affairs people to confiscate imperial weigh scales, to issue fines as high as $5,000 on summary conviction to people who continue to use imperial weigh scales, and, if all this fails, to use its right through order in council to sentence to jail terms, in other words, to put retail merchants in Canada in prison.
The minister responded by saying that the government had received the co-operation of the private sector on the implementation of metric. That is not the case, Mr. Speaker. It is misrepresenting the facts as they pertain to the implementation of metric in the retail food sector. If the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe) had been perfectly honest when he answered the question, he would have
advised the House that the president of the Canadian Federation of Retail Grocers said that they did not wish to move to metric in the retail grocery stores of Canada prior to the United States moving to metric. We know that the United States Congress has decided not to go metric in the retail food sector for at least ten years and maybe never.
If he had been perfectly honest, the minister would also have advised the House that Loblaws Companies Limited, which represent over 15,000 retail outlets in Canada, including 307 corporate stores and 1,300 affiliate franchise supermarkets, has advised both the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) as follows:
We feel strongly that cost justification must be shown prior to the implementation of the metric system in the retail food industry.
If the minister were perfectly honest with the people of Canada and this House of Commons, he would have responded that the Working Group on Scales in the food industry, a volunteer group of retail merchants and consumers, had the following to say:
The retail food industry members of the Working Group wish to recommend strongly to the government that the scheduling of retail food scale conversion to metric units in Canada, which appeared in The Canada Gazette Part I of 28 February, 1981, be delayed so that conversion will take place at a time closer to when retail food scales will be converted in the United States.
If the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs were perfectly honest, they would have reported to the House that Pat Carson, the corporate manager for Loblaws, has stated that it will cost between $2.5 million and $3 million to convert scales in their stores alone. He added that it would be irresponsible not to say that the cost would have to be borne by the consumer, and for that reason they are opposed to metric in the retail food sector.
The minister has not told the whole story about consumers either. The Peterborough Examiner of May 11 reported on a survey by retail merchants in the grocery business which showed that if the government goes ahead with the legislation, it will be against the will of the public. Surveys have been taken by Dominion Stores in Peterborough and Sherbrooke where the pilot studies were conducted which indicate overwhelming opposition to metric at this time when the United States is not going metric.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that we are not getting the correct information from the minister in question period. On October 26 The Wall Street Journal reported that the United States metric board has been told by the Reagan administration that it is walking its last mile. The United States is going back to using miles on highway signs, to Fahrenheit on the national weather service, and will deal in inches and feet.
I have a letter from the minister responsible for consumer affairs in the British government which states that the British government has abandoned the compulsory element in metrication and is letting the pace of change be voluntary in the remaining sectors of trade and industry and up to the individual firms or industries directly concerned.
November 9, 1981

I should like to know why the minister continues to mislead this House and to bring in orders in council which will lead to fines, imprisonment and confiscation of equipment under a program which in the beginning was voluntary, at the choice of the sectors as they moved into metric.
Instead, the government has taken it upon itself to force metric on the retail food sector. None of the evidence supports metric for the retail food sector, and I challenge the minister or his representative in the House tonight to name one organization, one business group or one retail outlet that supports metric for fruit, vegetables, meat and fish. As you know, Mr. Speaker, 70 per cent of our trade is with our American partners to the south and they have no intention of going metric in the retail food sector.
Of all the countries that agreed to go metric in 1971, when this House also agreed, not one is left. Britain has abandoned its metric commission, Mr. Reagan has given his commission until March 1, 1982 to fire everyone connected with it. There is no longer to be a metric commission in the United States to implement the metric system by force.
Why do we, representing 7 per cent of the population of North America, march into metric against the will of consumers, against the will of retail grocers, against the will of consumer groups, and, I can assure you, if we were all to be honest, Mr. Speaker, against the will of the majority of members in the House?
Therefore, would the minister please give us some facts? He should not continue to mislead us by saying that 95 per cent of the world is going metric in retail food. That is a lot of nonsense. The fact is that some of the world has gone metric, but not by force, not by regulation, and not by order in council. It has gone forward because it has been to the advantage of some countries to go metric, whether in the automotive industry or whatever. They have not gone metric because some cabinet members behind closed doors have passed an order in council threatening them with jail terms, fines and imprisonment if they do not advertise and use only SI-Systems International-French metric, eliminating all forms of imperial measure here in Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gary F. McCauley (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: METRIC CONVERSION-SUGGESTED PENALTIES FOR FOOD STORE OWNERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) has made a number of statements and assertions, most of which are open to question. He has cast doubt on the answer that the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe) made to his question in the House on November 4. I am not here to represent that minister who is quite capable of answering for himself; but I would like to respond, in particular, to the charges that the hon. member for Peterborough has made concerning Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
I must say that I am puzzled as to what document the hon. member is referring to when he suggests that it is the intention of this government to jail those who do not comply with the
Adjournment Debate
regulations governing metric conversion in the retail sale of individually measured foods. I can tell the hon. member that it will be the responsibility of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to enforce these regulations made under the Weights and Measures Act in exactly the same manner as all other such regulations are enforced.
The hon. member may be interested in knowing that our well established inspection practice involves first, informing non-complying retailers of their obligations under the law, in this case to advertise and sell individually measured foods as required by these regulations. Then, we encourage the retailers to take whatever action is necessary to comply with the regulations. Should a retailer not take action to comply with the regulations, he would be advised in writing that continued non-compliance would result in the initiation of prosecution action.
Should a retailer be prosecuted for non-compliance with these regulations, I might point out that the highest penalty that could be imposed for cases such as these would be a maximum fine of $1000, for each offence-not $5,000, if I understood the hon. member correctly. I might also point out that devices would only be seized in those instances where it would be required in the gathering of evidence for enforcement action.
I would also like to assure the hon. member that we do not anticipate that extensive enforcement action will be required to ensure compliance with these regulations. We have every confidence that retailers of individually measured foods will convert to metric as required commencing January 4, 1982. Surely, the hon. member realizes that Canadian retailers have been, are and will be good corporate citizens who will obey the law.

subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION-CHARTER PROPOSALS ON LANGUAGE RIGHTS
THE CONSTITUTION-CHARTER PROPOSALS ON LANGUAGE RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 23, of last month, the Ottawa Citizen and the Montreal Gazette stated on their front pages that the minority language provisions for education found in Section 23 of the constitutional proposals would be weakened to make them compatible with Bill 101 in Quebec. When I read those headlines in the newspapers that morning, I was shocked and upset. I came to the House at two o'clock in the afternoon and put a question to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien). I asked him whether it was true that the government intended to weaken minority language provisions for education in order to get an agreement with Quebec on the Constitution. The Minister of Justice answered me by stating that he was committed to minority language education for French and English-speaking Canadians on an equal basis throughout the country. He was not clear in stating whether or not the government intended to change Section 23 or weaken it in some way to get an agreement with the other provinces.

November 9, 1981
Adjournment Debate
Since that date, a lot of water has passed under the proverbial bridge. We now have an accord which was reached last week on November 5 between nine of the premiers and the federal government. While I congratulate them on that agreement, I am disappointed with a few provisions.
It is still not clear what language legislation will apply in Quebec with respect to education. While the nine premiers in the majority English-speaking provinces have agreed to the proposals in Section 23, and I must say that is quite an accomplishment, it is a first in Canadian history to have nine provinces agreeing to such a provision, on the other hand it is still not clear what will apply in Quebec. The government has said it will give some time to the government in Quebec to reconsider the provisions and perhaps negotiate some further settlement with Quebec.
First, I want to make it absolutely clear that in this controversial area I do not see how we can have one provision with respect to minority francophone rights applying in the nine majority anglophone provinces and something different applying in the province of Quebec. I do not think it would be acceptable to have two different provisions on language rights, one applying in Quebec and the other applying in the anglophone provinces.
Second, I do not see how we can retreat or weaken Section 23 to satisfy Quebec and therefore weaken it with respect to all of the other provinces as well when, as I say, for the first time all the anglophone provinces have agreed to such a provision. To backstep at this stage would be ridiculous and unacceptable in my view.
Premier Levesque, who is my premier, returned from the constitutional conference last week. He has stated, and he stated again this evening in the Quebec National Assembly, that he was betrayed by the other provinces and the federal government. He said that they ganged up on him and that this is just another example of English Canada stepping all over French Canada.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, and I will go over each point, how can it be said that English Canada is ganging up on French Canada when patriation has been agreed to? That was one of the items included in the accord. To the degree that the Constitution will be removed from Britain and made completely within the control of Canadians is that ganging up on Quebec?
Third, to accept an amending formula proposed by the government of Quebec with the seven other provinces, the so-called "Gang of Eight" even with the minor change, is that to be considered ganging up on Quebec? For the nine provinces and the federal government to agree to a charter with a provision whereby the provinces can override in many basic areas, can that be considered ganging up on Quebec?
Finally, when you have nine English-speaking provinces agreeing to what Mr. Levesque had proposed himself a couple of years ago, namely, that the other nine provinces agree to French-speaking education for the French-speaking minorities, how can you describe that as ganging up on the province of
Quebec when they agreed to French education in those English-speaking provinces? That is beyond me.
I again put it to the government and to the representative of the government who is here tonight that I can see no justification whatever for weakening Section 23, the section relating to minority language rights and education, or for applying something different in Quebec from what will apply in the other provinces. There is no justification for weakening that section or for applying something different in Quebec to what will apply in the other provinces. It was a great step forward for these other provinces to agree to what Mr. Levesque had proposed. Therefore, if he cannot see that, I am sure the people of Quebec will see it and will readily, once they have examined the proposals of this constitutional accord or agreement, see there is no such thing as ganging up on Quebec, but in fact that it is doing things that Quebec has asked for historically over many years.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Peterson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION-CHARTER PROPOSALS ON LANGUAGE RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to the question raised by my hon. colleague. The federal government has always supported, and continues to support, the principle of granting minority language education rights equally throughout this country. This is not the time that we intend to back off from that principle.
We have achieved a historic accord with nine provinces and the federal government, having agreed to patriation, an amending formula and a charter of rights which contains Clause 23 granting minority language education rights across this country.
We were all very disappointed to hear this afternoon and early evening that Premier Levesque has rejected our offer for further negotiations. He said he will not negotiate, he will intensify his lobby in London and he will henceforth boycott all federal-provincial conferences other than those which deal with Quebec's economy. This is most disappointing, particularly in light of the agreement he came to in terms of granting reciprocal language rights in St. Andrews in 1977.
As my hon. colleague asked in his question, how can it be said that we are ganging up on Quebec when we and the other provinces are prepared to grant reciprocal rights? How can it be said we are ganging up when the federal government announced that in order to try to reach some accommodation with the province of Quebec we would be prepared to enter into discussion on the three points which Mr. Levesque feels are contentious?
Dealing with the last of those three points, language rights, Mr. Ryan has proposed one type of possible alternative. As you are aware, it has always been our position, and it is contained in the charter, that the federal government and the provinces would allow access to English-speaking schools in Quebec whether or not the parents received their schooling in Canada. Mr. Ryan has proposed an alternative which is called the "Canada Clause". The Canada Clause would allow access
November 9, 1981

to English schools in Quebec to those children of Canadian citizens who received their primary school instruction in Canada. This is a slight change to what we have been proposing. It would have very limited application. We have indicated, as the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) has indicated, we would be prepared to consider this if it were to be acceptable to the government of Quebec. We are attempting to achieve an accord with the province of Quebec so that all ten
Adjournment Debate
provinces can go with the federal government to London to get our Constitution back.
